11240:
Before defining nominalism, you need to understand the problem it responds to, because without that context, the definition won't mean much. The problem is called the problem of universals, and it goes like this:

Look at a red apple, a red fire truck, and a red rose. You naturally call all three things "red." But why are you able to do that? What do those three things actually share?

Two possible answers exist:

Answer 1 — Realism: Those three objects all share a real, independently existing property called "redness." Redness is a universal — it exists as a genuine thing in the world, and each of those objects "has" or "participates in" it. When you call something red, you're pointing to this real, independent property.

Answer 2 — Nominalism: There is no such thing as "redness" floating around in the universe. The apple, the truck, and the rose don't share anything metaphysically real. What they share is only a name — the word "red." We humans noticed that these things look similar to us, so we invented a label for them. The label is useful and convenient, but it doesn't correspond to any independently existing thing in the world.

Nominalism is Answer 2.

Nominalism is the philosophical position that abstract concepts and general categories do not exist as real, independent things in the world. They are merely names — labels we attach to groups of similar individual things. Only concrete, particular, individual things truly exist.

The word to lock onto here is names. The nominalist sees words like "redness," "humanity," "beauty," "justice," and "the number five" as exactly that — names. Useful inventions of human language and thought. Not real things that exist independently out there in the world.

You have three pets: a golden retriever, a dalmatian, and a poodle. You call all three "dogs."

Now ask yourself: is there a thing called "dogness" — some essential property of being a dog — that exists independently of those three individual animals? Or did you simply observe that those three animals are similar enough to each other and decided to put them all under one convenient label: "dog"?

The nominalist says: there is no free-floating "dogness." The word "dog" is a label we invented for a group of similar creatures. Only the individual animals — this retriever, that dalmatian — are real. The category "dog" is just a name.

Now extend this logic to everything abstract. "Humanity," "triangularity," "the number five," "beauty," "justice" — none of these are real, independently existing things. They are names, concepts, and mental constructs. Only individual humans, individual triangles, individual beautiful objects are real.

The direct opposite of nominalism is realism (also called Platonic realism or universalism). Realists believe that abstract properties and categories — called universals — genuinely exist as real, independent things, separate from individual objects and separate from human minds.

Plato, the ancient Greek philosopher, is the most famous realist. He argued that for every category — beauty, justice, redness, triangularity — there exists a perfect, abstract "Form" in a non-physical realm. The beautiful things we see in the world are imperfect copies of the Form of Beauty. The triangles we draw are imperfect copies of the Form of Triangle.

Nominalism is, in large part, a rejection of exactly this kind of thinking. The nominalist says: there are no Forms, no abstract realm, no universals. There is only the physical world of individual things, and the names we attach to groups of them.

There is a third position sitting between realism and nominalism called conceptualism, and it's worth knowing because it helps sharpen what nominalism is saying.

Conceptualists say: universals exist, but only as mental concepts inside our minds — not as independently existing things out in the world. So "redness" is real as a concept in your head, but it doesn't exist independently of minds out there in nature.

Nominalism is stricter than this. For the nominalist, even calling a universal a real mental concept is saying too much. Universals are just names — linguistic labels — and nothing more. Nominalism locates universals entirely in language, not in the mind.

In practice, the line between nominalism and conceptualism gets debated, and some thinkers use the terms differently. But the key distinction is: nominalism says universals are just words or names; conceptualism says they are at least real ideas in the mind.

Nominalism is not a single rigid view — it's a family of related positions. Here are the main ones, in increasing sophistication:

Predicate Nominalism — The simplest version. A thing belongs to a category simply because a certain label or predicate applies to it. This apple is "red" just because the word "red" can correctly be applied to it. There's no deeper explanation needed. No shared property, no resemblance required — just the fact that the label fits.

Resemblance Nominalism — A more refined version. Things are grouped under the same name because they resemble each other. The apple, truck, and rose are all called "red" because they look similar to each other in a certain way. There is no universal "redness" — but the real resemblance between individual things is what justifies using the same name for all of them. For many people, this is the most intuitive version of nominalism, because it gives a reason for why we group things together beyond just "we invented a label."

Trope Nominalism — This version says that properties do exist, but they are not shared universals. Instead, each individual thing has its own unique, private instance of a property, called a trope. The redness of this specific apple is one individual instance of redness. The redness of that specific fire truck is a completely different individual instance of redness. These are two separate, particular things — not two objects sharing the same universal "redness." There are only individual things with individual private properties. The name "red" is what we use to group together all these individual redness-instances that resemble each other. No shared universal is needed.

Class Nominalism — A thing is red simply because it belongs to the class (or set) of red things. The class is just a collection. "Redness" is just a name for that collection. This avoids positing any universal property by replacing it with the notion of a set or class.
Why It Matters: Implications Across Different Fields

The debate between nominalism and realism isn't abstract puzzle-solving with no real-world stakes. It has significant consequences.

Mathematics — Do numbers exist as real things? A realist (called a Platonist in mathematics) says yes — the number 5 exists independently of human minds, just waiting to be discovered. A nominalist says no — "5" is a useful symbol and label we invented. There is no Platonic realm where numbers float around independently. This is one of the liveliest debates in the philosophy of mathematics today.

Science — When scientists classify animals into species, or matter into elements, are those categories real natural divisions in the world? Or are they useful labels humans invented? A realist says "tiger" as a species points to something genuinely real in nature. A nominalist says "tiger" is just a label humans invented to group similar-looking animals. There is no metaphysical glue binding all tigers together beyond our grouping of them.

Ethics and Morality — Is "justice" a real thing that exists in the world, waiting to be discovered? Moral realists say yes. Nominalists tend to say that "justice" is a concept humans invented — a name we give to certain arrangements and actions that we approve of. This deeply shapes how we think about whether moral truths are objective or constructed.

Religion and Theology — In medieval philosophy, debates about God's nature, the Trinity, and the soul were deeply tied to the nominalism vs. realism debate. This is one reason the debate was extraordinarily fierce in the Middle Ages — it wasn't just academic, it had religious consequences.

Language and Meaning — If category words like "dog," "red," or "justice" don't point to real things, then what exactly is language doing when we use such words? Nominalism forces us to think carefully about how words get their meaning and how communication works.

Plato (428–348 BC) — The great realist. Argued for the existence of abstract Forms as the most real things in existence.

Roscellinus (c. 1050–1125) — An early and radical nominalist who argued that universals are nothing more than puffs of air — mere sounds made by the human voice.

Peter Abelard (1079–1142) — A significant medieval thinker who argued against strong realism and held a position close to conceptualism. Often discussed alongside the nominalism debate.

William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) — The most famous and influential nominalist in history. He argued powerfully that universals exist only in the mind as mental concepts, and have no reality outside of it. He is also famous for Ockham's Razor — the principle that we should not multiply entities beyond what is necessary. His nominalism is a direct application of this: don't invent universals as extra, unnecessary entities when all you need are individual things and their names.

Nelson Goodman and W.V.O. Quine — Two major 20th-century analytic philosophers who defended forms of nominalism and made the debate central to modern philosophy.

"Nominalism means names don't matter or language is unimportant." Not at all. Nominalists take names very seriously — the entire point is that names are doing all the work. The claim is that categories are made of names and concepts, not that names are trivial.

"Nominalism means abstract concepts are fake or useless." No. The nominalist isn't saying "don't use the word 'redness' — it's meaningless." They're saying "redness" is a useful and legitimate name we apply to certain things, but there is no independently existing property called redness that the name "tracks." The name is useful; the claim is just about what kind of thing it refers to.

"Nominalism is obviously correct/obviously wrong." Neither. This is one of the oldest, most deeply contested debates in all of philosophy. Brilliant thinkers on both sides have been arguing about it for over two thousand years. Both positions have genuine strengths and face serious challenges.
The Summary, All in One Place

Nominalism is the philosophical position that only individual, concrete, particular things truly exist. Abstract concepts, general categories, and properties — like "redness," "justice," "humanity," or "the number five" — are not real, independently existing things in the world. They are merely names (labels) that we humans apply to groups of individual things that we perceive as similar. The word "red" does not point to a real universal property called redness existing independently in the universe — it is a useful label we invented for things that look similar to us.

Nominalism stands in direct opposition to realism, which holds that such universals are real and independent. It is also stricter than conceptualism, which says universals are at least real mental concepts, even if not things in the external world.

Within nominalism itself, the main variants differ on why we group things together: predicate nominalism says the label just applies; resemblance nominalism says the individual things genuinely resemble each other; trope nominalism says each thing has its own private property-instance; and class nominalism says membership in a set is all there is. All of them agree on the essential point: no universals, only particulars and names.
11241: A nominalist is a philosopher who believes that abstract categories and general concepts — things like redness, beauty, humanity, or justice — do not exist as real, independent entities in the world. To a nominalist, these are nothing more than names or labels that human beings invent to group similar things together.
The Question a Nominalist is Answering

To understand what a nominalist believes, you first need to understand the philosophical problem they are addressing. It is called the problem of universals, and it is one of the oldest debates in all of philosophy.

Here is the problem: Look at a red apple, a red fire truck, and a red rose. All three are red. They clearly share something. But what exactly is that shared thing?

Is redness — as a general property — a real feature of the world that actually exists somewhere? Or is it just a convenient label we invented to describe things that look similar?

That is the question. The answer a philosopher gives places them either in the realist camp or the nominalist camp.
The Two Opposing Views

Realists believe that universals like redness or humanity genuinely exist — not just as words in our heads, but as real features of reality, independent of any particular red thing and independent of any human mind. The ancient Greek philosopher Plato developed the most famous version of this view. He called these real, universal things Forms. On his account, Redness as a Form would still exist even if every red object in the universe were destroyed.

Nominalists reject this entirely. They say: there is no abstract entity called Redness floating in some non-physical realm. What exists are only concrete, individual things — this apple, that truck, this rose. Each is its own unique, particular thing. The word red is simply a label humans use to collect things that look similar. The label is useful for communication, but it does not point to any real, independently existing thing beyond the individual objects themselves.

Put simply: for a realist, categories are part of the furniture of the universe. For a nominalist, categories are labels stuck on the furniture by human minds.
A Concrete Example

Take the concept of "dog." There are millions of individual dogs — a German Shepherd, a Chihuahua, a Golden Retriever, a Poodle.

A realist would say there is a real universal — dogness, or the essence of being a dog — that all of these animals genuinely share. This essence is a real feature of the world, not just a human idea.

A nominalist would say: there is no such thing as dogness lurking inside these animals or existing somewhere else. There are only individual animals. We group them under the name dog because they physically resemble each other, behave similarly, and share an evolutionary lineage. But dog is simply our name for the group — a practical label, and nothing more. The world itself does not come pre-sorted into categories called dog and cat and tree. We impose those divisions through language.
The Simplest Way to Think About It

A nominalist essentially believes: the world contains things, not categories. Categories are something we project onto the world through our language and thought. A realist believes the opposite: the world actually contains real categories and properties as part of its structure, independent of what we think or say.
The Middle Ground: Conceptualism

It is worth knowing that there is a third, intermediate position called conceptualism, most closely associated with the medieval philosopher Peter Abelard. A conceptualist agrees with the nominalist that universals do not exist independently out in the world, but disagrees that they are merely arbitrary names. Instead, a conceptualist says universals exist as concepts or mental structures in the mind — real within thought, even if not real out in the external world. Nominalism, by contrast, tends to deny even that much independent reality to universals.
Why This Debate Matters Beyond Classrooms

This might seem like a purely abstract game, but nominalism touches some very significant real-world questions:

Mathematics. Do numbers actually exist? A nominalist about mathematics says numbers like 7 or concepts like infinity are not real abstract objects — they are useful fictions, tools we invented to describe the world. A mathematical realist (often called a Platonist) says numbers genuinely exist independently, the way physical objects do. This remains a live and unresolved debate among mathematicians and philosophers today.

Science and biology. When biologists classify organisms into species like Homo sapiens or oak tree, a nominalist says these species categories are human-invented groupings — useful for organizing observations, but not representing any deeper, real boundary in nature. A realist says the categories reflect genuine divisions that exist in nature itself.

Ethics. Does justice exist as a real thing, or is it just a name we give to patterns of behavior we happen to approve of? Nominalism, applied to morality, suggests moral categories are human constructions rather than mind-independent features of the universe.

Everyday language. Even ordinary words like chair, game, fruit, or color raise nominalist questions — do these words carve the world at its real joints, or are they just convenient, somewhat arbitrary labels?
The Varieties of Nominalism

Nominalism is not a single, uniform doctrine. There are different ways of being a nominalist, and they vary in how exactly they explain what is really going on when we group things under a common name.

Predicate Nominalism is the strictest version. When we call many things red, the only thing they truly have in common is that the word red applies to all of them. There is no deeper similarity among them that makes them really belong together — just the shared label.

Resemblance Nominalism is more generous. Things we group under one name — like red — genuinely resemble each other, and that resemblance is why we use the same label for them. But what ties them together is their resemblance to one another, not some shared universal property. The resemblance is real; the universal is not.

Trope Nominalism takes a distinct approach. It says that individual properties do exist — but only as unique, one-of-a-kind instances. The redness of this specific apple is its own unique property-instance, entirely distinct from the redness of that specific fire truck. What we call Redness (the universal) is actually just many distinct individual instances of red that we loosely group together. These individual property-instances are called tropes. Trope nominalism is influential in contemporary philosophy.

Class Nominalism says that when we say something is red, all that means is that it belongs to the class (or set) of all red things. The class is defined simply by which things are in it — not by any universal property.

All of these varieties share the core conviction: there is no universal abstract entity called Redness or Dogness or Justice that exists independently of the particular things we apply those words to.
Famous Nominalists

The battle between nominalists and realists was one of the most intense controversies in medieval philosophy, roughly between the 11th and 14th centuries.

Roscelin of Compiègne (c. 1050–1125) is often considered one of the earliest explicit nominalists. His views were considered so radical by the Church that he was condemned at the Council of Soissons in 1092.

William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) is the most celebrated nominalist in history. This English philosopher and friar argued powerfully that we should not invent unnecessary abstract entities to explain the world. This principle became known as Ockham's Razor — roughly, do not multiply entities beyond what is necessary. If you can explain why we call things red without inventing a universal called Redness, then you should not invent it. Ockham's Razor became one of the most enduring methodological principles in science and philosophy.

In modern philosophy, Nelson Goodman (1906–1998) was a rigorous and committed nominalist. W.V.O. Quine (1908–2000), one of the most influential philosophers of the 20th century, was at least sympathetic to nominalism, particularly about abstract mathematical objects, though his position evolved over time.
A Misconception to Avoid

In everyday English, the word nominal sometimes means very small (a nominal fee) or existing in name only (a nominal leader who holds the title but has no real power). While this everyday usage is distantly connected to the philosophical concept, it is not what nominalist means.

A nominalist, as a noun, always refers specifically to someone holding the philosophical position described above — never to something that is merely token or trivially small.

Also: a nominalist has nothing to do with making nominations, as in political nominations. That is a completely unrelated word.
Summary

A nominalist is a philosopher who believes that only individual, particular things are genuinely real — this apple, this dog, this person. Abstract general categories and properties (called universals) — like redness, beauty, humanity, or justice — do not exist as real, independent entities in the world. They are nothing more than names or labels that human beings use to group together individuals that resemble each other or share some common feature. The world, for a nominalist, contains things — not categories. The categories are our own invention, tools of language and thought, not features of reality itself.
11242: "Nominally" means "in name only." When something is described as nominally being a certain thing, it means the label, title, or official description says one thing — but the reality tells a different story. It always points to a gap between what something is called and what it actually is.
Feel It With a Simple Example

Imagine your friend is technically the "captain" of a football team, but he never leads the group, doesn't show up to practice, and the coach ignores him completely. You'd say:

"He is nominally the captain."

He has the title. On paper, he's the captain. But in reality, he isn't doing what a captain does. That's exactly what "nominally" signals — the name is there, the substance is not.
More Examples to Lock It In

"She is nominally the CEO, but her co-founder runs everything."
The title belongs to her. The actual power does not.

"The country is nominally at peace, but clashes happen every week."
Officially, there is no war. In practice, violence continues.

"He nominally works in accounting, but spends most of his time on sales."
His official department is accounting. His actual work is elsewhere.

"The organization is nominally independent, but the government controls its budget."
It claims independence. But true independence doesn't exist.

Notice the pattern in every sentence: something has an official status, but the reality doesn't match that status. "Nominally" is always doing the same job.

Every time you see "nominally," it is signaling: the official name or label is true only on the surface. Dig a little deeper, and reality is different.

You can think of "nominally" as a quiet warning: don't be fooled by the label.

This is why journalists and writers love this word. When someone writes "the prime minister nominally heads the committee," you immediately know something is off — the real power lies somewhere else. The word carries subtle irony, a hint that the title is almost a fiction.

"Nominally" also has a second meaning, mostly in formal, technical, or scientific writing: "to a very small degree" or "barely."

Here it describes something so small or trivial that it almost doesn't count.

"The two proposals are nominally different." — They differ, but only by a negligible amount.

"The cost increased nominally." — The price went up, but by so little it barely matters.

This meaning is rare in everyday speech. You'll mostly encounter it in economics, science, or academic writing. The spirit is still the same: something exists, but only barely — to such a small degree that you might question whether it's really there at all.
How the Two Meanings Are Connected

Both meanings share the same underlying idea: something exists only technically. Whether it's a title that exists only on paper, or a difference so tiny it might as well not exist — "nominally" is always pointing to a gap between the formal truth and the meaningful, practical truth. In both cases, the word hints: this thing is real in the most technical sense, but don't read too much into it.

Understanding what a word isn't is just as useful as knowing what it is.

"Nominally" ≠ "mostly." If someone is nominally in charge, they are barely in charge — not mostly in charge. The word leans toward the hollow end of a thing, not the full end.

"Nominally" ≠ "apparently" or "seemingly." Those words express uncertainty about whether something is true. "Nominally" doesn't question the label — it accepts the label but questions the reality behind it. The title is real. What's in doubt is whether the title means anything.

"Nominally" ≠ "officially." "Officially the leader" simply means the record confirms it — no shadow is cast on it. "Nominally the leader" casts a direct shadow: the record says leader, but don't expect real leadership.

The word "nominal" is built around the idea of a name — a designation, a label, a title. So "nominally" = in the manner of just a name. Something is nominally X when all that really exists is the name X, not the full, real, meaningful thing that X is supposed to represent.

Every time you see "nominally," ask yourself: What's the gap here? What is it called, and what is it actually? That question will always unlock the meaning.

"Nominally" is a word that reveals the distance between a label and a lived reality. It acknowledges a title, a status, or an official description — and then immediately questions whether that description reflects the truth. It is precise, a little cynical, and enormously useful for describing the world as it actually is, rather than how it is officially presented.
11243:
To nominate someone means to officially put their name forward as a candidate — for an award, a position, a role, or a responsibility. Think of it as formally raising your hand and saying, "This person should be considered."

The most important thing to understand right away: nominating is not the same as choosing or selecting. It is the step that comes before the final decision. You place someone in the running. What happens next — a vote, an approval, a panel's decision — determines the outcome.
The three main ways "nominate" is used

1. To put someone forward as a candidate in a competition or selection process

This is the most common use. After nomination, a separate process decides the outcome.

  • "She was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize." — She was put forward as a candidate. Whether she wins is decided separately.
  • "I nominate James for class president." — James is now officially in the running. The vote comes next.
  • "The film was nominated for Best Picture." — It made the shortlist. The winner is announced later.

Being nominated in this sense is already meaningful on its own. It signals that someone believed you were worthy enough to be considered.

2. To formally propose someone for an official position (which then requires approval)

In government, law, and formal organizations, "nominate" often means a person in authority officially selects someone for a role — but that choice still needs to be confirmed or approved by another body.

  • "The president nominated her as Secretary of State." — The president chose her and put her name forward, but the Senate must still approve the appointment.
  • "The CEO nominated a new member to the board of directors." — A formal proposal was made; the board must vote to confirm.

Here, nominating carries more weight than a casual suggestion — it comes from someone with authority — but it is still not the final, binding step.

3. To designate someone for a task or purpose (with no competition involved)

Sometimes "nominate" simply means to officially assign or designate someone for something specific — with no voting or competitive element at all.

  • "Please nominate someone from your team to attend the workshop." — Just pick and name a person.
  • "You can nominate a beneficiary for your life insurance policy." — You officially name the person who will receive it.
  • "She nominated her colleague as the group's representative." — She designated him for that role directly.

In this use, nominating is effectively the final decision. There is no separate approval or vote — the act of nominating completes the process.

Mostly, people are nominated. But things — like films, books, songs, and companies — can also be nominated, especially for awards. Even in those cases, it still means they have been put forward as candidates and are now in the running.

• The person who nominates someone is called the nominator.
  • The person who has been nominated is called the nominee.
  • The act of nominating, or the state of having been nominated, is called a nomination.

"The nominees for Best Actress were announced this morning."
"His nomination to the Supreme Court sparked widespread debate."

The word almost always appears in one of these three patterns:

  • Nominate someone for something → "They nominated her for the award."
  • Nominate someone as something → "He was nominated as team leader."
  • Nominate someone to something → "She was nominated to the committee."
The single most important distinction to lock in

Nominating ≠ selecting. Nominating = officially putting someone forward to be considered, approved, or designated. The final outcome may be decided by an entirely different process — or in simpler situations, the nomination itself may be the end of it. Context tells you which one applies.

Once you understand that "nominate" always involves the official act of naming someone for something — and that this naming can range from a mere proposal all the way to a direct designation depending on the context — you have a complete grasp of this word.
11244:
A nomination is the formal act of putting someone forward as a candidate — as someone who should be considered for a position, role, honour, or award. It is a proposal that says: "This person deserves to be in the running."

The critical thing to understand from the start: a nomination is not a final decision. It is a step before the final decision. Being nominated means you have been officially entered into consideration. Whether you actually get the position or win the award is a separate matter that comes afterward.

Think of almost any important selection process — an election, an award ceremony, a job appointment. Rarely does someone just appear in the final seat out of nowhere. There is almost always a step where someone says, "I officially put this person's name forward." That act — that formal putting-forward of a name — is a nomination. And the result of that act (the state of having been put forward) is also called a nomination.

So the word carries two closely related senses:

  1. The act itself — the moment or process of formally proposing someone.
    "The nomination of a candidate must happen before the election."
  2. The resulting status or instance — the fact that someone has been proposed.
    "She received three nominations for best actress."

Both meanings are correct and common. Context tells you which one is meant.
Who Nominates and Who Is Nominated

A nomination always involves at least two parties:

  • The nominator — the person, group, or body that has the authority or right to put someone forward. This could be a political party, a committee, an organisation, a governing body, or even an individual with the standing to do so.
  • The nominee — the person who has been nominated. They are now officially in the running.

It is worth noting that a person can sometimes nominate themselves, though this is less common in formal settings. In such cases, they are both the nominator and the nominee.

The word nomination implies a degree of formality and officialness. It is not a casual suggestion made in conversation. When someone says "How about John for the job?" over coffee, that is an informal suggestion, not a nomination. A nomination happens within a structured process — there are rules, there is a recognised body that receives the nomination, and the nomination carries real weight because it officially places someone on a list of candidates.

This formality is what makes a nomination meaningful. It is a gatekeeping step: not everyone can be considered; only those who have been nominated enter the pool from which the final choice is made.
The Contexts Where You Will Encounter This Word

1. Politics and Elections
This is perhaps the most common context. Before a general election, a political party holds a process to decide which person will represent the party as their official candidate. This process is called a nomination process, and the event at which the candidate is formally chosen is often called a nomination. In some countries, this larger event is called a nominating convention.

"The party's nomination of its presidential candidate was announced last week."

Once nominated, the person becomes the party's nominee and goes on to compete in the actual election.

2. Awards and Competitions
In entertainment, arts, sports, and academia, organisations announce nominations before revealing winners. A film might receive a nomination for Best Picture at an awards ceremony. A musician might receive a nomination for Album of the Year. Being nominated is already considered an honour, because it means a respected body has formally recognised that person's work as deserving of consideration.

"The film received five nominations, including one for Best Director."

Note that you can receive multiple nominations — one for each category you have been put forward in.

3. Appointments to Positions
When governments, organisations, or institutions appoint people to important roles, the process often begins with a nomination. A president might nominate someone to serve as a judge. A board might nominate a person to serve as chairperson. In these cases, the nomination is a formal proposal that must then be approved or confirmed by another authority before the appointment becomes official.

"The president's nomination of a new Supreme Court justice must be confirmed by the Senate."

This is an important distinction: the nomination is the proposal, and the confirmation or approval is the finalisation. Until the second step happens, the person is merely a nominee, not yet in the role.
The Life Cycle of a Nomination

Understanding a nomination is easier when you see where it fits in a process:

  1. A need arises — a position opens up, an award cycle begins, an election approaches.
  2. Nominations are invited or made — eligible nominators formally put forward names.
  3. A shortlist of nominees exists — these are the people in contention.
  4. A selection is made — through voting, committee decision, or appointment.
  5. A winner or appointee is announced — one nominee succeeds; others do not.

A nomination lives at steps 2 and 3. Everything before it is background; everything after it is outcome.

Nomination vs. Election/Appointment
A nomination is a proposal; an election or appointment is the outcome. A person can be nominated many times and never win or be appointed. Equally, being nominated is not a guarantee of anything — it merely opens the door to possibility.

Nomination vs. Selection
Selection is the final choice. Nomination is what makes you eligible to be selected. You must typically be nominated before you can be selected.

Nomination vs. Application
In many processes, people apply for positions (they put themselves forward). In a nomination, someone else (or a body) puts you forward — though, as noted earlier, self-nomination exists in some contexts. The key difference is that a nomination carries the endorsement of the nominator, which gives it a different weight than a simple application.

• A nomination can be a form of recognition in itself. Especially in awards, being nominated signals that your work or contribution has been acknowledged by an authority, even if you do not win. This is why people say things like "It is an honour just to be nominated."
  • Nominations can be withdrawn. If a nominee declines, becomes ineligible, or if circumstances change, a nomination can be withdrawn before the final decision is made.
  • The word can refer to a single instance or a collective. "Her nomination was unexpected" refers to one specific act. "The nominations were announced today" refers to the full list of people nominated across all categories.
  • Nomination implies legitimacy. Because it happens within a formal process, a nomination carries official standing. It is not just any suggestion — it is a recognised, recorded proposal within an established system.

If you had to capture the whole idea in a single sentence: A nomination is the formal, official act of proposing someone as a candidate for a position, role, or award — placing them in contention without guaranteeing them the outcome.

It is the moment a door is officially opened for someone. What happens next — whether they walk through that door — depends on what follows.
11245:
A nominee is a person who has been officially named or put forward by someone — a person, a group, or an organization — for a specific purpose. That purpose is usually one of three things: to compete for an award, to run for a position, or to act on someone else's behalf.

The single most important thing to understand about a nominee is this: someone else did the naming. A nominee does not nominate themselves. Another person or body — called the nominator — is the one who says, "We choose this person." The moment that happens, the chosen person becomes a nominee.

Think of it this way. The word nominee comes from the act of nomination — which simply means the official act of naming someone for something. So a nominee is just "the person who was named."

If your school says, "We are putting forward Maria for the Student of the Year award," then Maria is the nominee. She didn't ask for it herself. The school named her. That's all it takes to be a nominee.

The word nominee is used in three major areas of life, and understanding each one will make you confident using it anywhere.

1. Awards and Recognition

This is perhaps the most familiar use. When a committee, academy, or organization selects a group of people who could win an award, each of those people is called a nominee.

"The five nominees for Best Film were announced last night."

Here, a panel has looked at all the films of the year and officially named five of them as candidates for the prize. Those five are the nominees. Only one will eventually win — but all five hold the title of "nominee" from the moment they are named until the winner is declared.

Key point: Being a nominee does not mean you have won. It means you have been officially considered and publicly recognized as someone deserving of the prize. It is an honor in itself, separate from actually winning.

2. Politics and Elections

In politics, a nominee is someone who has been officially chosen by a political party to represent that party in an election.

"She became the party's nominee for president after winning the primaries."

In many democratic countries, political parties go through an internal selection process to decide who will be their official candidate in a general election. The person they select at the end of that process is their nominee. This person then goes on to compete in the actual election against nominees from other parties.

Again, being a nominee here means you have been chosen and put forward — not that you have already won the election.

Sometimes, the word also applies when a head of state (like a president) officially proposes someone for an important government role, such as a cabinet minister or a judge. That proposed person is called a nominee until they are formally approved and confirmed.

"The president's nominee for Chief Justice will face a confirmation hearing next week."

In this case, the president has named (nominated) someone, but that person must still go through an approval process before they officially hold the role.

3. Legal and Business Affairs (Acting on Someone's Behalf)

This is a slightly different — and more technical — use of the word, but it is equally important to know.

In law and business, a nominee is a person or company that is officially named to act on behalf of someone else, usually to hold something — like property, shares, or a company position — in their name while the real owner or decision-maker stays in the background.

"The property was registered in the name of a nominee."

For example, imagine a wealthy investor who wants to buy shares in a company but doesn't want their name publicly associated with it. They can appoint a trusted person or a company — the nominee — to hold those shares officially in their name. The nominee's name appears on paper, but they act purely on the instructions of the real owner.

Common examples include:

  • A nominee director: A person whose name appears as a company director, but who acts on the instructions of the real controller.
  • A nominee shareholder: A person or company that holds shares on behalf of the actual, real owner.
  • A nominee account: A financial account held by a broker or institution in their own name, but on behalf of the actual investor.

Key point: In this context, the nominee is not acting for their own benefit. They are a kind of stand-in or placeholder — a trusted representative who holds or manages something on behalf of the person who appointed them.

1. A nominee is not the same as a winner.
In awards and elections, a nominee is someone who could win, not someone who has won. The winner was once a nominee, but not every nominee becomes a winner.

2. A nominee is not the person who does the nominating.
The person who nominates is the nominator. The person who receives the nomination — who is named — is the nominee. Always remember: the nominee is on the receiving end of the nomination.

3. A nominee is not always an individual person.
While we most commonly use the word for people, organizations and companies can also be nominees. For example, a production company could be a nominee for a business award.

4. A nominee is not necessarily confirmed or in place yet.
Especially in political and legal contexts, a nominee is someone who has been proposed or put forward but may still need approval, confirmation, or election before they fully take on the role.

SituationWhat "nominee" means
AwardsA person officially named as a candidate who could win
PoliticsA person officially chosen to run in an election, or proposed for an official role
Law/BusinessA person who holds something (property, shares, a role) on behalf of another

A nominee is always someone who has been officially named by another for a specific purpose — whether that's to compete for a prize, to represent a party, to fill a role, or to act on someone's behalf. The common thread is always the same: someone else named them, and that naming carries official weight.
11246:
A non sequitur is a statement, conclusion, or response that does not logically follow from what came just before it. There is a broken — or completely absent — logical connection between what was said and what comes next.

Think of it as a logical leap that makes no sense. You go from Point A, and instead of landing on Point B (where logic would take you), you land somewhere completely unrelated — Point Z, or some alien planet altogether.
The Two Main Worlds Where This Word Lives

1. In Logic and Argumentation

This is the word's most precise, technical sense. In logic, a non sequitur is a fallacy — a reasoning error — where someone states a conclusion that simply doesn't follow from their own evidence or premises.

Example:

"Maria practices yoga every day. Therefore, she would be an excellent surgeon."

The premise (practices yoga) has no logical path that leads to the conclusion (would be a great surgeon). The conclusion just appears out of nowhere, unjustified by the evidence given. That's a non sequitur.

Notice: the conclusion might happen to be true — maybe Maria is, in fact, a gifted surgeon. But that's beside the point. The argument is still a non sequitur because the reasoning doesn't hold. The conclusion isn't earned by the premise.

Another example:

"He drives an expensive car. He must be a trustworthy person."

Wealth and trustworthiness are completely different things. One doesn't logically follow from the other.

2. In Everyday Conversation

Outside of formal logic, a non sequitur refers to a remark that is completely disconnected from the topic being discussed — a statement that comes out of nowhere and has nothing to do with what's going on.

Example:

Person A: "We should leave by 6 PM to beat the traffic."
Person B: "Do you think fish dream?"

Person B's response has no relation to what Person A said. It's jarring, unexpected, and contextually out of place. That's a conversational non sequitur.

These pop up in real life when someone:

  • isn't paying attention and blurts out something unrelated,
  • has been thinking about something else entirely and accidentally says it aloud,
  • abruptly changes the subject without any bridge or transition.
When Non Sequiturs Are Intentional: Comedy and Surrealism

Not all non sequiturs are mistakes. Writers, comedians, and artists use them deliberately to create specific effects.

In comedy, a non sequitur is a powerful tool. The sudden, illogical jump catches you off guard, and the surprise itself is what makes you laugh. Much of absurdist humor (think Monty Python, or certain stand-up comics) is built almost entirely on non sequiturs.

Example of a comedic non sequitur:

"I told my doctor I broke my arm in two places. He told me to stop going to those places. Anyway, clouds are just sky sponges."

That last sentence is a deliberate non sequitur for laughs. You're not meant to connect it to anything — the disconnection is the joke.

In surrealist or experimental writing, non sequiturs are used to reflect the chaotic, dreamlike nature of thought, or to deliberately disorient the reader and create an unsettling, strange atmosphere.
The Key Thing to Always Remember

A non sequitur is not about whether a statement is true or false. It's about whether it follows logically from what precedes it.

  • "The sky is blue, therefore 2 + 2 = 4" → Both statements are true. But it's still a non sequitur because one has absolutely nothing to do with the other.
  • "She's a vegetarian, therefore she must be kind to animals" → This feels connected, but it's still a non sequitur — being a vegetarian doesn't automatically mean someone is kind to animals. The logical leap is unjustified.

The test is always: Does this conclusion/statement actually follow from what was just said? If no, it's a non sequitur.
How a Non Sequitur Differs from Similar Things

Non sequitur vs. a tangent: A tangent is when someone drifts slightly off topic, but there's usually still a loose thread connecting it to the original subject. A non sequitur has no connecting thread at all.

Non sequitur vs. a red herring: A red herring is intentionally used to distract or mislead someone (often in arguments or mysteries). A non sequitur may be accidental or intentional, but its defining feature is the logical disconnection, not the intent to deceive.

Non sequitur vs. a contradiction: A contradiction is when two statements clash and can't both be true. A non sequitur isn't about two statements clashing — it's about two statements having nothing to do with each other.

A non sequitur is any statement, conclusion, or response that doesn't logically or contextually follow from what came before it. The link between what was said and what follows is broken or nonexistent. It can be:

  • a logical fallacy in an argument (conclusion doesn't follow from the evidence),
  • an out-of-place remark in conversation (response doesn't connect to what was said),
  • or a deliberate comedic or artistic device that exploits the absurdity of disconnection.

The heart of the word is always the same: something that simply does not follow.
11247:
When something is non-negotiable, it means it is completely fixed and final. It cannot be changed, discussed, adjusted, or bargained about — no matter what. There is zero room for argument, compromise, or flexibility. It simply is what it is, and that is the end of the matter.

Think of it this way: imagine a wall made of solid rock. You can talk to the wall all you want, push against it, reason with it, beg it — but it will not move. That is what non-negotiable feels like. The thing in question is that wall.
Breaking Down the Logic of the Word

The word is built from two parts: non- (meaning "not") and negotiable (meaning "open to discussion or bargaining"). So literally, non-negotiable means not open to discussion or bargaining. If something is negotiable, you can talk about it, make offers, and arrive at a middle ground. Non-negotiable is the direct opposite of that. The conversation is over before it even starts.
What It Implies — the Feeling It Carries

Using the word "non-negotiable" signals absolute firmness. It tells the other person: "Do not even try to change this. My mind is made up, and no argument — however clever — will alter it."

It carries a sense of authority and finality. Whoever says it is drawing a hard line. There is often a subtle warning underneath it: if you push against this, you will be wasting your time, or there will be consequences.

It is one of the strongest words in English for expressing that something is immovable. Saying "I'd prefer this" is soft. Saying "I'd really like this" is firmer. Saying "this is non-negotiable" is the hardest, most absolute version — the final word.
The Two Main Worlds Where This Word Lives

1. Rules, policies, and formal settings

In workplaces, schools, governments, and legal agreements, certain rules are non-negotiable because they are fixed by law, policy, or authority. You cannot bargain with them. You cannot opt out.

Examples:

  • "Wearing a helmet on a construction site is non-negotiable — it is a safety rule."
  • "The tax deadline is non-negotiable; it applies to everyone."
  • "The contract has several non-negotiable terms that both sides must accept as they are."

In these cases, the rule exists above the individual. No single person has the power to change it through personal persuasion.

2. Personal values and boundaries

People also use "non-negotiable" to describe their own personal principles, limits, or standards — things they refuse to compromise on no matter the pressure or temptation. These are the things so important to a person that giving them up would feel like betraying themselves.

Examples:

  • "Respect is non-negotiable in my relationships. I will not stay where I am disrespected."
  • "For me, honesty is non-negotiable. I will not lie, even when the truth is uncomfortable."
  • "Spending Sunday mornings with my family is non-negotiable for me."

Here, the person is the one setting the rule — for themselves or for others dealing with them.

• "The manager told the team: the deadline is next Friday, and that is non-negotiable."
  • "Safety standards at the factory are non-negotiable and must be followed by every worker."
  • "She told him that her privacy was non-negotiable — he had to respect her boundaries."
  • "The terms of the peace agreement were described as non-negotiable by both governments."
  • "Getting eight hours of sleep is non-negotiable for me — my health depends on it."
  • "The entrance fee is non-negotiable; there are no discounts or exceptions."

You will very often see "non-negotiable" paired with certain words. The most common ones are: non-negotiable terms, non-negotiable conditions, non-negotiable demands, non-negotiable deadline, non-negotiable price, non-negotiable boundary, and non-negotiable rule.

The most common sentence pattern is simply: "This is non-negotiable." This phrase alone, spoken firmly, is enough to shut down any further discussion on a topic.

Non-negotiable is an adjective, so it describes a noun. You can place it before a noun ("a non-negotiable rule") or after a linking verb like is, are, was, remains ("the terms are non-negotiable").

You can also use it as a standalone noun when talking about personal values or conditions. For example: "Write down your non-negotiables before entering any partnership." Here, "non-negotiables" is being used as a noun meaning "the things you will absolutely not compromise on." This is a very common modern usage, especially in the context of self-improvement, relationships, and business.
What It is NOT — Sharpening the Definition Through Contrast

Understanding what non-negotiable is not will make the meaning sharper.

Something is not non-negotiable if there is any room at all for discussion or change. For instance, "I'd prefer to meet on Monday" is flexible — the day could change. But "Monday is non-negotiable for me" means Monday, and nothing else, period.

Non-negotiable is also different from merely being difficult to change. A price that is hard to negotiate is still technically negotiable — you could, in theory, strike a deal. A non-negotiable price means no deal is possible; the number is fixed, full stop.

The word can sometimes feel confrontational or heavy when used between people, because it completely removes the other person's ability to contribute their perspective. In casual conversation or close relationships, using it too often or too aggressively can come across as rigid or domineering. Context and tone matter.

However, it is also deeply empowering when used to protect one's own values or wellbeing. Knowing and stating your non-negotiables — especially in relationships, work, or personal life — is widely considered a sign of self-awareness and healthy boundaries.
Non-negotiable means something is completely fixed and final — it cannot be changed, questioned, or bargained about, no matter what, by anyone.
11248:
Nonage means the state or period of being not yet fully grown, legally capable, or mature — either as a young person who hasn't reached the legal age of adulthood, or more broadly, as anything (a person, an idea, an institution, a civilization) that hasn't yet reached its full, developed form.

Think of it as the "not yet there" stage of existence.

The word carries two closely connected meanings that share the same root idea:

1. The Legal Meaning (the original, stricter sense)

In law, nonage refers to the period of a person's life before they reach the age of majority — the age at which the law considers them a full adult, capable of making their own binding decisions.

During a person's nonage, the law treats them as not yet capable of full responsibility. This means they generally cannot:

  • Sign legally binding contracts
  • Make a valid will
  • Consent to marriage without a guardian's permission
  • Be tried as an adult in a court

The law essentially says: this person is still in their nonage — they don't yet have the full legal standing of an adult.

In older legal systems (particularly English common law), nonage often meant the period before age 21. In most modern legal systems, it refers to the period before age 18, though this varies by country and by the specific right or responsibility in question.

Example: "The contract was void because one of the parties was in his nonage at the time of signing."

This is the word's most precise and historically important meaning.

2. The Figurative (Extended) Meaning

The second meaning takes the idea of "not yet fully mature" and applies it far more broadly — not just to people, but to anything that is still in an early, undeveloped, or immature phase.

This is where the word becomes especially powerful and expressive. You can use nonage to describe:

  • A field of knowledge or science that is still young and not yet fully established
  • An art movement that hasn't yet reached its peak
  • A civilization or nation that is still in its early stages of development
  • A person's intellectual or emotional maturity, even if they are legally an adult
  • An industry, technology, or institution that is still forming and finding its shape

Example: "In the nonage of cinema, directors were still figuring out how the medium worked."
Example: "His philosophy, though brilliant, was clearly still in its nonage — the ideas hadn't yet been tested or fully refined."

In this figurative sense, nonage is essentially a synonym for "infancy" or "early stage," but with a slightly more formal, literary feel and with an added implication of limited capability or incomplete development, not just youth.

Both meanings of nonage are really one idea seen in two contexts:

Nonage = a state of being not yet fully developed, capable, or mature.

Whether you're talking about a 15-year-old who can't legally vote, or a brand-new scientific discipline that hasn't yet established its core theories — both are in a state of nonage. They exist, they have potential, but they haven't arrived at their full form yet.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Nonage is a formal word. You will encounter it in:

  • Legal texts and historical legal documents
  • Academic writing (philosophy, history, literary criticism)
  • Formal or literary prose

You would almost never hear it in casual, everyday conversation. If someone uses this word, they are being precise, formal, or deliberately literary. It carries a slightly elevated, intellectual tone — which is part of what makes it useful when you want to express the idea of "immature early stage" with a kind of dignified seriousness.

It's worth clearing up a few potential confusions:

  • It does not mean "no age" in a literal sense (as in, ageless or timeless). Despite how it might look, it specifically means the period before full maturity, not the absence of age.
  • It is not simply a synonym for "childhood." Childhood is a biological and social concept. Nonage is a more precise concept anchored in capability, legal standing, or developmental completeness. A 17-year-old is not a child in the typical sense, but is still technically in their nonage.
  • It is not the same as "minority" in the racial or social sense. In legal language, "minority" and "nonage" overlap and are sometimes used interchangeably, but both in that context refer only to being under the age of majority — not to demographic identity.

What it isA state or period of being not yet fully mature, developed, or legally capable
Legal senseThe period before reaching the legal age of majority (typically before 18 or 21)
Figurative senseThe early, undeveloped stage of anything — a field, a civilization, an idea, a person's mind
ToneFormal, literary, precise
Key feeling of the word"Not yet arrived at its full form"

If you remember one thing: nonage is the "not yet fully there" phase — whether that's a young person not yet recognized by law as a full adult, or any idea, institution, or endeavor that is still in its early, unfinished state.
11249:
A nonagenarian is a person who is between 90 and 99 years old — not a day younger than 90, and not yet 100. The moment someone turns 90, they become a nonagenarian. The moment they turn 100, they are no longer one.

Think of it as a label for a specific "decade of life" — just like how we might casually say someone is "in their thirties," a nonagenarian is someone who is formally "in their nineties."

This is important to get right:

  • A person who is 89 → not yet a nonagenarian
  • A person who is 90, 91, 92 … all the way to 99 → a nonagenarian ✓
  • A person who is 100 → no longer a nonagenarian (they are now a centenarian)

So the word covers exactly 10 possible ages: 90, 91, 92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97, 98, and 99.

The word is used to describe or refer to a person of that age range. It works exactly like the word "teenager" does for someone aged 13–19, or "toddler" for a very young child. It is a single, precise word that tells you everything about which stage of life a person is in — without having to say "a person in their nineties."

Example sentences:

  • "The nonagenarian celebrated her 95th birthday surrounded by four generations of family."
  • "As a nonagenarian, he still walked two miles every morning."
  • "The interview featured three nonagenarians who had lived through two world wars."

Notice how in each case, the word replaces a longer phrase and carries very specific age information with it.

English has a neat set of words, all built on the same pattern, each covering one decade of older life. Knowing them together makes each one much easier to remember:

  • Quadragenarian — someone in their 40s (40–49)
  • Quinquagenarian — someone in their 50s (50–59)
  • Sexagenarian — someone in their 60s (60–69)
  • Septuagenarian — someone in their 70s (70–79)
  • Octogenarian — someone in their 80s (80–89)
  • Nonagenarian — someone in their 90s (90–99) ← that's our word
  • Centenarian — someone who is 100 or older
  • Supercentenarian — someone who is 110 or older

Seeing this list makes it clear that "nonagenarian" sits right near the top of human lifespan — one step below a centenarian, making it a word associated with remarkable longevity.

1. It is age-specific, not health-specific.
A nonagenarian can be frail or extraordinarily fit. The word says nothing about someone's health, mobility, or mental sharpness. It only tells you their age. A 94-year-old marathon runner and a 94-year-old in a care home are both equally nonagenarians.

2. It is neutral and respectful.
The word carries no negative connotation. It is not a polite way of saying "very old and declining." It is simply a factual, clinical, and dignified descriptor of age — often used in journalism, medicine, and formal writing.

3. It requires being alive in that range.
If someone died at 88, you would never call them a nonagenarian. The word describes a living person's current age, or historically, the age a person had reached during their lifetime.

4. It is not commonly used in everyday casual conversation.
You would rarely hear a grandchild say, "my grandma is a nonagenarian." In daily speech, people say "she's 93" or "she's in her nineties." The word "nonagenarian" tends to appear in news articles, medical literature, biographies, historical writing, and formal speeches, often to lend a note of gravity or distinction to someone's advanced age.

If you ever forget this word, here is a simple trick: the word contains "nona" — think of "nine" (like how "November" was once the ninth month in the old Roman calendar). Nona → Nine → Nineties. That connection alone is enough to reconstruct the meaning on the spot.
A nonagenarian is simply a person who has lived to be somewhere between 90 and 99 years old — a word used to mark that rare, remarkable stretch of human life with precision and respect.
